why: Evidence: over 120s / 9785 requests the canary (v1.1, 2411 reqs) is indistinguishable from stable (v1.0, 7374 reqs) on every headline metric. Errors: 0 5xx and 0.00% err% on both sides - no new failure mode appeared under ~25% of real traffic. Latency: canary p50 34ms vs stable 34ms, p95 93ms vs 94ms, p99 105ms vs 104ms. Per route the medians and p95s match within 1ms: /browse 22/27 vs 22/27, /search 47/59 vs 47/59, /checkout 82/104 vs 81/103. The checkout path, the most revenue-critical and slowest route, shows no regression (462 canary reqs, 0 errors, p99 107ms vs 105ms). Stability over time: canary p95 by window is 92, 92, 93, 96 against stable 94, 94, 95, 92, and 5xx stays at 0 in all four windows - no error onset, no memory/leak-style upward drift that would show as a climbing tail. One anomaly, stated plainly: canary /browse p99 is 77ms against stable 28ms. Judgement: this is a thin tail affecting roughly the slowest 1% of 1200 requests (~12 requests) on the cheapest route, while that same route's p95 is identical at 27ms and the absolute value (77ms) is still well under the service-wide p95; most likely cold-start or JIT/cache warm-up on a single fresh pod rather than a systemic regression. Judgement: that is not a customer-visible harm large enough to block a release, so the cost asymmetry (bad promote hurts customers vs bad rollback blocks a release) does not favor rolling back here. Caveats: the canary is a single pod, so this test cannot reveal problems that only appear at 100% traffic (connection-pool, downstream, or dependency saturation), and 2411 requests with 0 errors only bounds the error rate loosely - roughly below ~0.12% at 95% confidence, so a rare fault could still hide. Recommended follow-up: promote progressively rather than in one jump, and watch /browse p99 and the 5xx rate at each step; roll back if /browse p99 does not settle toward the stable ~28ms once the new pods are warm, or if any 5xx appears.
